## cfoai
# cfo.ai MCP

You are connected to **cfo.ai** — an AI-native financial planning workspace. This MCP exposes Ari's public product tools for you to call directly. You can both **read** a company's financial model and **change** it: create and edit scenarios, pages, table blocks, Canvas blocks, formulas, variables, dimensions, and data ingestion.

Model-editing tools change the live model immediately and record reversible changes in its
changelog. Connections, access changes, and outbound actions have effects outside model undo. Build from saved data, research, supplied numbers, estimates, hypotheses, or invented
assumptions. Clearly label uncited inputs and their basis in the model and handoff. Create missing
model objects and editable inputs as part of the work. A missing source citation does not block modeling.

## Read the reference before you build

cfo.ai has its own modeling method, described under "How a table shows the model" below: how tables show variables, dimensions, and fields, how a reference reads from the cell it sits in, and how a table's rows and columns are built. `inspect_skills` owns the built-in and workspace skill catalog. Use its `list` block to find a skill and its `instructions` block to read it.

Read `build-model` before creating or changing model logic, variables, dimensions, or saved tables;
`build-visualizations` before adding a Canvas block; and `import-model` before rebuilding a model
from a workbook or export. Each manual contains its complete reference in `SKILL.md`.

Workspace skills hold company-specific playbooks. Read the relevant saved guidance before substantial work.

## Calling convention

- A multi-action tool selects one operation with the block named for that action; single-purpose tools use their fields directly. Supply only fields supported inside the selected block. An `inspect_*` tool reads saved product state; an `edit_*` tool changes it.
- `target` identifies an existing object where the operation needs one, including the destination of a new block. Creation field… [truncated]

## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>

<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>

<?claude block s1?>

<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.

## claude.ai Higgsfield
Recipe/setup slashes: get_preset_instructions before other workflows; unambiguous model slashes: models_explore; unknowns: resolve. For 3D scenes or location angles, first call get_preset_instructions with { preset: "/3d-jutsu" }. This includes new camera views of the same supplied location; image critique alone does not activate scene work. After verifying a completed Katana video, call show_result with action "katana_video" and media_id or url. For /effects or Viral browsing use get_presets source:'viral'; /product or product-shot catalogs: source:'marketing_studio', category:'product-shot'; /motion or motion catalogs: category:'motion'. /marketing-studio opens get_presets source:'marketing_studio'. - Filter with `glob` (e.g. "**/*.tsx") or `type` (e.g. "js", "py", "rust").
- `output_mode`: "content" (matching lines), "files_with_matches" (paths only, default), or "count".
- `multiline: true` for patterns that span lines.

pattern.description: The regular expression pattern to search for in file contents

path.description: File or directory to search in (rg PATH). Defaults to current working directory.

glob.description: Glob pattern to filter files (e.g. "*.js", "*.{ts,tsx}") - maps to rg --glob

output_mode.description: Output mode: "content" shows matching lines (supports -A/-B/-C context, -n line numbers, head_limit), "files_with_matches" shows file paths (supports head_limit), "count" shows match counts (supports head_limit). Defaults to "files_with_matches".

-B.description: Number of lines to show before each match (rg -B). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-A.description: Number of lines to show after each match (rg -A). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

context.description: Number of lines to show before and after each match (rg -C). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-n.description: Show line numbers in output (rg -n). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to true.

-o.description: Print only the matched (non-empty) parts of each matching line, one match per output line (rg -o / --only-matching). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to false.

type.description: File type to search (rg --type). Common types: js, py, rust, go, java, etc. More efficient than include for standard file types.

head_limit.description: Limit output to first N lines/entries, equivalent to "| head -N". Works across all output modes: content (limits output lines), files_with_matches (limits file paths), count (limits count entries). Defaults to 250 when unspecified. Pass 0 for unlimited (use sparingly — large result sets waste context).

offset.description: Skip first N lines/entries before applying head_limit, equivalent to "| tail -n +N | head -N". Works across all output modes. Defaults to 0.

multiline.description: Enable multiline mode where . matches newlines and patterns can span lines (rg -U --multiline-dotall). Default: false.

tools.name: PowerShell
tools.description:
Executes a given PowerShell command with optional timeout. Working directory persists between commands; shell state (variables, functions) does not.

IMPORTANT: This tool is for terminal operations via PowerShell: git, npm, docker, and PS cmdlets. DO NOT use it for file operations (reading, writing, editing, searching, finding files) - use the specialized tools for this instead.

PowerShell edition: Windows PowerShell 5.1 (powershell.exe)
   - Pipeline chain operators `&&` and `||` are NOT available — they cause a parser error. To run B only if A succeeds: `A; if ($?) { B }`. To chain unconditionally: `A; B`.
   - Ternary (`?:`), null-coalescing (`??`), and null-conditional (`?.`) operators are NOT available. Use `if/else` and explicit `$null -eq` checks instead.
   - Avoid `2>&1` on native executables. In 5.1, redirecting a native command's stderr inside PowerShell wraps each line in an ErrorRecord (NativeCommandError) and sets `$?` to `$false` even when the exe returned exit code 0. stderr is already captured for you — don't redirect it.
   - `>`, `>>`, and `Out-File` usually default to UTF-8 (with BOM) in this environment, but `Set-Content`/`Add-Content` still default to the system ANSI codepage — when writing a file other tools will read, pass `-Encoding utf8` explicitly to `Out-File`/`Set-Content`.
   - `ConvertFrom-Json` returns a PSCustomObject, not a hashtable. `-AsHashtable` is not available.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:
   - If the command will create new directories or files, first use `Get-ChildItem` (or `ls`) to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location

2. Command Execution:
   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes
   - Capture the output of the command.

PowerShell Syntax Notes:
   - Variables use $ prefix: $myVar = "value"
   - Escape character is backtick (`), not backslash
   - Use Verb-Noun cmdlet naming: Get-ChildItem, Set-Location, New-Item, Remove-Item
   - Common aliases: ls (Get-ChildItem), cd (Set-Location), cat (Get-Content), rm (Remove-Item)
   - Pipe operator | works similarly to bash but passes objects, not text
   - Use Select-Object, Where-Object, ForEach-Object for filtering and transformation
   - String interpolation: "Hello $name" or "Hello $($obj.Property)"
   - Registry access uses PSDrive prefixes: `HKLM:\SOFTWARE\...`, `HKCU:\...` — NOT raw `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\...`
   - Environment variables: read with `$env:NAME`, set with `$env:NAME = "value"` (NOT `Set-Variable` or bash `export`)
   - Call native exe with spaces in path via call operator: `& "C:\Program Files\App\app.exe" arg1 arg2`

Unix commands that DO NOT exist in PowerShell — use the equivalent instead:
   - head / tail → `Get-Content file -TotalCount N` / `-Tail N`; piped: `| Select-Object -First N` / `-Last N`
   - which → `(Get-Command name).Source`
   - touch → `if (-not (Test-Path path)) { New-Item -ItemType File path }` (NEVER use `New-Item -Force` on a file — it truncates existing content)
   - wc -l → `(Get-Content file | Measure-Object -Line).Lines`
   - mkdir -p → `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force path` (`-p` is not a PowerShell flag)
   - rm -rf → `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force path`
   - ln -s → `New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink -Path link -Target target`
   - chmod / chown → not applicable on Windows; use `icacls` only if ACL changes are required
   - 2>/dev/null → `2>$null` (but stderr is captured for you — usually unnecessary)
   - VAR=x cmd → `$env:VAR = 'x'; cmd` (PowerShell has no inline env-var prefix)
   - Bash control flow (`if [ -f x ]`, `for x in *`, backtick ``cmd`` substitution) is a parser error — use `if (Test-Path x)`, `foreach ($x in ...)`, `$(cmd)`

Exit-code note: `-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` suppresses error OUTPUT but the cmdlet failure still causes this tool to report exit 1. To make a cmdlet failure truly non-fatal, promote it to terminating and swallow it: `try { Cmdlet ... -ErrorAction Stop } catch {}` (without `-ErrorAction Stop`, non-terminating errors skip the `catch` and still exit 1).

Interactive and blocking commands (this tool runs with -NonInteractive and stdin attached to the null device — console prompts read EOF or error immediately; GUI prompts can still block until timeout):
   - NEVER use `Read-Host`, `Get-Credential`, `Out-GridView`, `$Host.UI.PromptForChoice`, or `pause`
   - Destructive cmdlets (`Remove-Item`, `Stop-Process`, `Clear-Content`, etc.) may prompt for confirmation. Add `-Confirm:$false` when you intend the action to proceed. Use `-Force` for read-only/hidden items.
   - Never use `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`, or other commands that open an interactive editor

Passing multiline strings (commit messages, file content) to native executables:
   - Use a single-quoted here-string so PowerShell does not expand `$` or backticks inside. The closing `'@` MUST be at column 0 (no leading whitespace) on its own line — indenting it is a parse error:
<example>
git commit -m @'
Commit message here.
Second line with $literal dollar signs.
'@
</example>
   - Use `@'...'@` (single-quoted, literal) not `@"..."@` (double-quoted, interpolated) unless you need variable expansion
   - For arguments containing `-`, `@`, or other characters PowerShell parses as operators, use the stop-parsing token: `git log --% --format=%H`

Usage notes:
  - The command argument is required.
  - You can specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes for a foreground command). If not specified, commands will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
  - It is very helpful if you write a clear, concise description of what this command does.
  - If the output exceeds 30000 characters, output will be truncated before being returned to you.
  - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes. With `run_in_background` the timeout is instead how long the command may run in the background (default 1800000ms / 30 minutes, max 7200000ms / 2 hours); at that limit it is stopped and you are notified.
  - Avoid using PowerShell to run commands that have dedicated tools, unless explicitly instructed:
    - File search: Use Glob (NOT Get-ChildItem -Recurse)
    - Content search: Use Grep (NOT Select-String)
    - Read files: Use Read (NOT Get-Content)
    - Edit files: Use Edit
    - Write files: Use Write (NOT Set-Content/Out-File)
    - Communication: Output text directly (NOT Write-Output/Write-Host)
  - When issuing multiple commands:
    - If the commands are independent and can run in parallel, make multiple PowerShell tool calls in a single message.
    - If the commands depend on each other and must run sequentially, chain them in a single PowerShell call (see edition-specific chaining syntax above).
    - Use `;` only when you need to run commands sequentially but don't care if earlier commands fail.
    - DO NOT use newlines to separate commands (newlines are ok in quoted strings and here-strings)
  - Do NOT prefix commands with `cd` or `Set-Location` -- the working directory is already set to the correct project directory automatically.
  - Avoid unnecessary `Start-Sleep` commands:
    - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
    - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — simply run your command using `run_in_background`. There is no need to sleep in this case.
    - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause or consider an alternative approach.
    - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
    - If you must poll an external process, use a check command rather than sleeping first.
    - If you must sleep, keep the duration short to avoid blocking the user.
  - For git commands:
    - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
    - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
    - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Required unless `stop` is true.

stop.description: Set to true to end the dynamic loop immediately instead of scheduling another wakeup. When true, all other fields are ignored and no further wakeups fire.

noop.description: true = nothing changed (you checked and there is nothing to report). false = something happened worth keeping (edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, surfaced a finding). I'm checking which MCP tools apply: Higgsfield for media generation, t3-code for screen recording the app UI, preview tools for driving the Electron app, and cfoai MCP for setting up the real scenario. content.text:
I pulled frames from the Melty video. It's a 30s, 1080p30 cut, and almost all of it is **real footage with motion-graphic overlays**. There's very little AI-generated video in it. The structure is:

1. A 3D curved wall of game cover cards. Two get picked, then a "Mash with AI" pill appears.
2. A terminal showing the MCP tool calls, with a numbered checklist that animates in beside it ("Looked up… / Built… / Tested on your PC").
3. Real gameplay with a title chip in the corner ("Elden Ring x Jump Force"), plus a webcam reaction.
4. A marketplace grid ("Just released", "New remixes").
5. Back to the card wall, which blurs out behind the logo and URL.

Your script fits that template well. It has 5 beats instead of 4, so plan for about 45–60s.

## What you already have connected

| Need | Tool | Used for |
|---|---|---|
| Recording the Benana UI | **t3-code** `preview_open` / `preview_click` / `preview_type` + `preview_recording_start/stop` | Scripted, repeatable recordings of the Build page, Neatlogs/Entire panels, Marketplace and CFO page. This replaces hand-recording the screen. |
| AI-generated b-roll and stills | **Higgsfield** `generate_image`, `generate_video`, `upscale_video`, `remove_background` | Beat 1, "modding before Benana": a frustrated dev, a mess of Java/Gradle errors, crash logs. Also Minecraft-style backgrounds and the card art for the wall. |
| Voiceover and music | **Higgsfield** `generate_audio` (+ `create_voice` for a consistent narrator) | VO for each beat and the backing track |
| Checking pacing | **Higgsfield** `video_analysis_create` | Analyse the Melty video (or your own cut) for shot timing |
| CFO beat | **cfoai** MCP (`edit_scenarios`, `edit_canvas_blocks`) | Build a real "creator feasibility" scenario so the footage shows live numbers instead of a mock |

## What you'd need to add

1. **Remotion itself.** It needs no MCP, only `npx create-video@latest` in a `launch-video/` folder. It's worth adding Remotion's docs MCP (`@remotion/mcp`) and their agent skills (`remotion-dev/skills`) so I write current Remotion APIs (`<Sequence>`, `<TransitionSeries>`, `@remotion/three` for the card wall, `@remotion/media-utils` for audio sync). I believe both exist but haven't checked those package names yet.
2. **Capturing the real Minecraft client.** This is the one real gap, because the preview tools only record web pages. Options:
   - **OBS + an obs-websocket MCP** (best): I can start and stop recording around the agent's test run, so the capture is synced to the build.
   - **ffmpeg `gdigrab`** through Bash. You already have ffmpeg 8.1 installed, so this works with no extra setup, just less control.
3. **Optional: ElevenLabs MCP**, if Higgsfield's voices aren't good enough for the narrator.

## How each beat would be made

| Beat | Footage source | Remotion layer |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Modding pain | Higgsfield b-roll + mock IDE/Gradle-error UI | Kinetic type, "hours → weeks" counters, error stack cascade |
| 2. Agent builds a mod | t3-code recording of BuildPage + OBS clip of the BlackHoleGrenade in the real client | Melty-style numbered checklist animating in next to the terminal, title chip on gameplay |
| 3. Stuck → Neatlogs + Entire | Recording of the agent hitting an error, the Neatlogs trace, and an Entire checkpoint restore | Callout arrows, a "stuck" freeze-frame, a timeline rewind effect |
| 4. Marketplace on Entire | Recording of MarketplacePage + checkpoint hover | Animated checkpoint graph: a mod forks from a checkpoint, then another user builds on it |
| 5. cfo.ai | Recording of CfoPage with a real cfoai scenario | Number tickers, feasibility verdict, then the logo outro over the blurred mod wall |

Two things to sort out before we record:
- My memory notes say your Neatlogs ingest key was invalid as of today. Beat 3 needs real traces, so that has to be fixed first.
- The working tree has uncommitted CFO and marketplace changes, so the recordings would show work in progress.

If you're good with this, the first steps are to scaffold the Remotion project and write a shot list with VO lines and timings. Do you want to add OBS, or should I use ffmpeg for the Minecraft capture?

entries.description: Get the user's available credits and current subscription plan. For transaction history, call `transactions` instead.

entries.name: mcp__claude_ai_Higgsfield__generate_audio
entries.description: Generate one speech/voice request (text-to-speech) and render it in the generation widget. This tool accepts one prompt; for 2-12 independent lines or prompts, use the headless generate_audio_batch tool instead. DEFAULT model: seed_audio (Seed Audio 1.0 by ByteDance) — use it unless the user explicitly asks for a different engine. seed_audio takes a preset or reference-element voice (voice_type 'preset'|'element' + voice_id) plus optional tuning params (format, sample_rate, speech_rate, loudness_rate, pitch_rate), and can clone a voice from an audio_references media item or take an image_references cue. To use a specific named engine instead, set model:'text2speech_v2' and pass variant (one of elevenlabs|minimax|seed_speech|vibe_voice|cozy_voice) together with voice_type + voice_id. Get voice ids from list_voices; use models_explore(type:'audio') to inspect each model's params. This tool only generates speech: it cannot generate music or sound effects for general use, and there is no standalone music/SFX model here — decline general music or sound-effect requests rather than substituting a speech model. The models sonilo_music (music), mirelo_text_to_audio (sound effects) and inworld_text_to_speech (voice) exist ONLY for the game-generation pipeline and must not be used for standalone audio. get_cost:true preflights credits without submitting. use_unlim defaults false — pass true only when the user explicitly asks to use their unlimited/free-trial generations, never to save them credits on your own initiative. Submitted audio requests can send text and reference inputs to external audio model providers through Higgsfield and consume credits. On a transport timeout the submission outcome may be unknown: do not automatically resubmit. Reuse returned job IDs and retry only after the original outcome is known.

folder_id.description: Destination folder for this conversation. Use default_folder_id from create_project, or folder_id from create_folder when requested. Reuse on every generation and batch item in this conversation; never invent an ID or share a destination across chats. Omit by default for generation without a project. Before the first generation without a destination, call get_preferences: create a project only when auto_create_project is true or explicitly requested. Explicit existing destinations and requests to work without a project take priority; never change the saved preference for a one-off request.

model.description: Audio model ID from the model catalog (required). Use models_explore(type:'audio') to discover.

prompt.description: Text prompt for the generated audio.

count.description: One result for this prompt. Use generate_audio_batch for independent lines or prompts.

voice.description: Voice for inworld_text_to_speech. Use models_explore(type:'audio') to inspect allowed values.

voice_type.description: For seed_audio and text2speech_v2: whether voice_id is a built-in preset voice ('preset') or a workspace reference element ('element').

voice_id.description: For seed_audio and text2speech_v2: the preset voice id (voice_type='preset') or reference element id (voice_type='element').

value.description: UUID from media_upload/media_import_url or job_id from a prior generation. Do not pass https:// URLs here.

role.description: Role — varies by model; inspect the selected model's medias[].roles. Server may auto-coerce when unambiguous.

duration.description: Duration in seconds. Required for sonilo_music and mirelo_text_to_audio; omit for the text-to-speech models.

get_cost.description: If true, return the cost in credits for this generation without submitting any job. Use to preflight cost before generating.

use_unlim.description: Which balance pays for this generation: the caller's free-trial unlimited generations (true) or their credits (false). OMIT IT to let the server decide — if they hold an allowance that covers the model, the tool submits nothing and returns `unlim_choice`, the question to put to the user before spending anything of theirs. Answer it by calling again with the same params plus this field; the answer is remembered for a few minutes, so a multi-step flow is asked once. true also caps count to 1. Whichever way it is set, a rejected opt-in is reported rather than quietly replaced with a charge.

context.description: Briefly describe the user's underlying goal and why this call helps, in one short sentence. Do not include names, contact details, credentials, URLs, or biometric details. Analytics only; not a generation prompt.

entries.name: mcp__claude_ai_Higgsfield__models_explore
entries.description: Find generation models. Use recommend with goal + input context; use get for model constraints. Items carry supports_unlim when the model accepts free-trial unlimited generations; the top-level unlim block says whether the caller can spend them right now, and the trailing 'Unlim configs' text lists the configurations their allowance actually covers.

query.description: Model/use-case query; include input context like text-only, reference image, image-to-video, or product URL.

type.description: Filter by output type (omit to include all)

input.description: Input filter: image = accepts reference media; text = text-only.

unlim.description: When true, return only models that accept free-trial unlimited generations (supports_unlim). Use it to answer "which models can I use my unlimited generations on" in one call — each returned item still carries its aspect_ratios, parameters, and durations. Omit to include all models; false is the same as omitting it.

limit.description: Max results, default 20 for list/search, 5 for recommend

after.description: Pagination cursor (next_page_token from a previous list/search result; not used by recommend)

content.thinking: I'll use a Monitor to watch for completion instead of polling, checking the Monitor tool's schema and setting a watch condition for text like "passed every check" or "Failed"/"attempt" in the body, while I continue building the Remotion scenes in parallel.

entries.name: Monitor
entries.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, until the monitor expires (re-arm to continue)** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). Every monitor expires after `timeout_ms` (default 5 minutes, at most 30 minutes): it is killed and you get one notice with the event count. Re-arm it if you still need the watch; for a long watch (PR monitoring, log tails) set `timeout_ms` to the maximum and re-arm on each expiry, and widen the filter if an expiry with no events was unexpected. Use TaskStop to cancel early.
**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

Each text frame becomes one notification (multiline frames stay as one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]` rather than passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code surfaced; errors are surfaced before close. Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.

description.description: Short human-readable description of what you are monitoring (shown in notifications).

timeout_ms.description: Kill the monitor after this deadline. Default 300000ms. Deadlines above 1800000ms are capped to 1800000ms. You are notified at expiry and can re-arm.

command.description: Shell command or script. Each stdout line is an event; exit ends the watch.

ws.description: WebSocket to open. Each text frame is an event; binary frames are reported as a placeholder line. Socket close ends the watch. Cannot be combined with command.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Cuts the OBS recordings in footage/ into the clips the video uses (public/footage/*.mp4).
# Each segment is "file start end speed"; app captures lose the 24px Electron menu bar.
set -euo pipefail
cd "$(dirname "$0")"

clip() { # clip <out> <crop:0|1> <segment>...
  local out=$1 crop=$2; shift 2
  local inputs=() filters="" labels="" i=0
  for seg in "$@"; do
    read -r file start end speed <<<"$seg"
    inputs+=(-ss "$start" -to "$end" -i "footage/$file")
    local c=""; [ "$crop" = 1 ] && c="crop=1920:1056:0:24,scale=1920:1080,"
    filters+="[$i:v]${c}setpts=(PTS-STARTPTS)/$speed,fps=30,format=yuv420p[v$i];"
    labels+="[v$i]"; i=$((i+1))
  done
  ffmpeg -v error -y "${inputs[@]}" -filter_complex "${filters}${labels}concat=n=$i:v=1:a=0[out]" -map "[out]" \
    -c:v h264_nvenc -preset p5 -cq 19 -g 15 "public/footage/$out.mp4"
  echo "$out $(ffprobe -v error -show_entries format=duration -of csv=p=0 public/footage/$out.mp4)s"
}

content.content:
1	# Benana Mod Studio
2	
3	Describe a Minecraft mod in one sentence. Benana writes it as a Paper plugin, starts a Minecraft server inside the app, and sends an AI player in to test it. When the playtest fails, a fixer agent reads the in-game evidence, patches the plugin, and the AI player tests it again.
4	
5	![Benana Mod Studio: the agent's report on the left, the live game, server log, Neatlogs traces and Entire checkpoints on the right](docs/images/build.png)
6	
7	## Start with one sentence
8	
9	> "A golden sword that launches any mob it hits into the sky with particles, with a 3 second cooldown."
10	
11	Type an idea, or pick one of the examples, and press Enter. You never open an IDE, a server console, or the game client. Lessons the fixer has learned from earlier mods are shown under the examples and passed to every new build.
12	
13	![The New mod composer with example ideas and the lessons the fixer has learned so far](docs/images/new-mod.png)
14	
15	## What happens next
16	
17	1. **Spec agent** (Claude Opus) turns the sentence into behavior rules and an in-game **test plan** with measurable expectations, for example "the husk's upward velocity exceeds 0.8 blocks/tick".
18	2. **Builder** (Claude Code, Opus) implements the plugin in its own git repository created from `templates/paper-plugin`, and Maven builds it.
19	3. **Deploy**: Benana restarts its local Paper 1.21.4 server with the new jar, which takes about 16 seconds.
20	4. **Playtester** (Claude Code, Sonnet) controls `BenanaBot`, a real player, through the `minecraft` MCP tools: equip, attack, use items, and track an entity's velocity tick by tick. It reports pass, fail, or blocked for each check, with the measurements as evidence.
21	5. **Fixer** (Claude Code, Opus) receives the verdict, server stack traces, the mod's Entire checkpoint history, and the Neatlogs trace of the failed playtest. It fixes the root cause, writes down a **lesson**, and the loop runs again (up to 3 attempts).
22	
23	## Watch the AI player test it
24	
25	The live view is a real Minecraft 1.21.4 client, spectating next to BenanaBot, so you see the playtest with the game's own rendering: particles, lightning, the mod's textures and boss bars. The bot gets the item, spawns a target, and uses the mod on it. The server log streams next to it, so plugin errors are visible as they happen.
26	
27	## Play it yourself
28	
29	**Play in Minecraft** opens a second real Minecraft window and drops you into the same world, next to the bot, holding the mod's items (and husk eggs for targets). Benana downloads the vanilla client files from Mojang the first time and joins Benana's local server with them. Set `BENANA_PLAYER_NAME` in `.env` to pick your name.
30	
31	![Three frames from BenanaBot's first-person view as it fights husks in the test arena](docs/images/live-view.png)
32	
33	## When a playtest fails, it fixes itself
34	
35	A failed check is not the end of the run. Every attempt keeps the measured evidence, the agent sessions behind it, and the fixer's lesson.
36	
37	The **Mods** page below shows ArrowTracer, a real run that needed three attempts. The request was "can't see the arrows being shot". The first build reported the arrow's landing spot 1.3 blocks from the shooter instead of 7 to 9. The fixer traced the impact point along the arrow's velocity and wrote that down as a lesson. The second playtest still failed. On the third attempt the fixer worked out that the plugin was right: the husk had walked up to the bot before the shot. It fixed the test target by giving it NoAI, and all four checks passed. Total cost: $1.32.
38	
39	![The Mods page: ArrowTracer's spec and its attempt timeline, with failed attempts, evidence and the fixer's lesson](docs/images/mods.png)
40	
41	## Every agent session is traced (Neatlogs)
42

file.content:
# Benana Mod Studio

Describe a Minecraft mod in one sentence. Benana writes it as a Paper plugin, starts a Minecraft server inside the app, and sends an AI player in to test it. When the playtest fails, a fixer agent reads the in-game evidence, patches the plugin, and the AI player tests it again.

![Benana Mod Studio: the agent's report on the left, the live game, server log, Neatlogs traces and Entire checkpoints on the right](docs/images/build.png)

## Start with one sentence

> "A golden sword that launches any mob it hits into the sky with particles, with a 3 second cooldown."

Type an idea, or pick one of the examples, and press Enter. You never open an IDE, a server console, or the game client. Lessons the fixer has learned from earlier mods are shown under the examples and passed to every new build.

![The New mod composer with example ideas and the lessons the fixer has learned so far](docs/images/new-mod.png)

## What happens next

1. **Spec agent** (Claude Opus) turns the sentence into behavior rules and an in-game **test plan** with measurable expectations, for example "the husk's upward velocity exceeds 0.8 blocks/tick".
2. **Builder** (Claude Code, Opus) implements the plugin in its own git repository created from `templates/paper-plugin`, and Maven builds it.
3. **Deploy**: Benana restarts its local Paper 1.21.4 server with the new jar, which takes about 16 seconds.
4. **Playtester** (Claude Code, Sonnet) controls `BenanaBot`, a real player, through the `minecraft` MCP tools: equip, attack, use items, and track an entity's velocity tick by tick. It reports pass, fail, or blocked for each check, with the measurements as evidence.
5. **Fixer** (Claude Code, Opus) receives the verdict, server stack traces, the mod's Entire checkpoint history, and the Neatlogs trace of the failed playtest. It fixes the root cause, writes down a **lesson**, and the loop runs again (up to 3 attempts).

## Watch the AI player test it

The live view is a real Minecraft 1.21.4 client, spectating next to BenanaBot, so you see the playtest with the game's own rendering: particles, lightning, the mod's textures and boss bars. The bot gets the item, spawns a target, and uses the mod on it. The server log streams next to it, so plugin errors are visible as they happen.

## Play it yourself

**Play in Minecraft** opens a second real Minecraft window and drops you into the same world, next to the bot, holding the mod's items (and husk eggs for targets). Benana downloads the vanilla client files from Mojang the first time and joins Benana's local server with them. Set `BENANA_PLAYER_NAME` in `.env` to pick your name.

![Three frames from BenanaBot's first-person view as it fights husks in the test arena](docs/images/live-view.png)

## When a playtest fails, it fixes itself

A failed check is not the end of the run. Every attempt keeps the measured evidence, the agent sessions behind it, and the fixer's lesson.

The **Mods** page below shows ArrowTracer, a real run that needed three attempts. The request was "can't see the arrows being shot". The first build reported the arrow's landing spot 1.3 blocks from the shooter instead of 7 to 9. The fixer traced the impact point along the arrow's velocity and wrote that down as a lesson. The second playtest still failed. On the third attempt the fixer worked out that the plugin was right: the husk had walked up to the bot before the shot. It fixed the test target by giving it NoAI, and all four checks passed. Total cost: $1.32.

![The Mods page: ArrowTracer's spec and its attempt timeline, with failed attempts, evidence and the fixer's lesson](docs/images/mods.png)

## Every agent session is traced (Neatlogs)

Every builder, playtester, and fixer session is traced through `@neatlogs/claude-code` hooks installed into each mod repository. The **Neatlogs** page lists all sessions across all mods. Opening one shows its cost, tokens, the failure it was handed, each tool call, and its final output. The fixer reads the failed playtest's trace before it changes any code.

![The Neatlogs page with the ArrowTracer fixer session open: duration, tokens, cost, the attempt 2 failure it received, and its 7 steps](docs/images/neatlogs-trace.png)

## Every commit is tied to its session (Entire)

Each agent commit in a mod repository carries an `Entire-Checkpoint` trailer that links the code to the session that wrote it. The **Entire** page shows the commit history per mod: builder, playtest, and fixer commits in order, with the checkpoint that produced each one. The fixer gets this history as context.

![The Entire page: ArrowTracer's six commits, alternating fixer attempts and playtests, each linked to a checkpoint](docs/images/entire.png)

## Insights

The **Insights** page tracks build outcomes, pass rate, first-try passes, and spend broken down by agent role and model.

![The Insights page: mods built, pass rate, agent sessions, total spend, build activity and spend by agent role](docs/images/insights.png)

## Partner tools

- **Neatlogs** traces every agent session (see above).
- **Entire** checkpoints every attempt (see above). This repository has Entire enabled too.
- **cfo.ai** holds the business plan: [docs/hackathon/cfo-plan.md](docs/hackathon/cfo-plan.md).

## Run it

Requirements: Node 22+ on `PATH` (the game bot runs on system Node), JDK 21, Maven 3.9, and Claude Code logged in. Install the [Entire CLI](https://github.com/entireio/cli) and `npm i -g @neatlogs/claude-code` for partner evidence.

```sh
npm ci
cp .env.example .env     # add Neatlogs keys
npm run dev
```

Click **Start game**, describe a mod, and press Enter. On first start Benana downloads Paper (51 MB). Game data lives in `~/.benana/game`, mod repositories in `~/.benana/mods`.

- `BENANA_GAME_AUTOSTART=1` starts the game with the app. `BENANA_GAME_DEMO=1` turns on attract mode, where the bot keeps launching husks. `BENANA_VIEW=first` switches the live view to the bot's first-person camera.
- **Seeded bug** (the toggle under the prompt) starts from `fixtures/seeded`, a labeled LaunchSword with the knockback bug. The playtester and fixer still run for real, and the UI labels the run as seeded.
- If Electron crashes at startup with `reading 'handle'`, unset `ELECTRON_RUN_AS_NODE`.

```sh
npm run build
npm test
```

Architecture and interfaces: [docs/hackathon/CONTRACTS.md](docs/hackathon/CONTRACTS.md). Build plan: [docs/hackathon/PLAN.md](docs/hackathon/PLAN.md). The original repository-bug workspace is still available from **Repository workspace** in the sidebar; see [execute_yourself.md](execute_yourself.md).

# Benana Mod Studio

Describe a Minecraft mod in one sentence. Benana writes it as a Paper plugin, starts a Minecraft server inside the app, and sends an AI player in to test it. When the playtest fails, a fixer agent reads the in-game evidence, patches the plugin, and the AI player tests it again.

![Benana Mod Studio: the agent's report on the left, the live game, server log, Neatlogs traces and Entire checkpoints on the right](docs/images/build.png)

## Start with one sentence

> "A golden sword that launches any mob it hits into the sky with particles, with a 3 second cooldown."

Type an idea, or pick one of the examples, and press Enter. You never open an IDE, a server console, or the game client. Lessons the fixer has learned from earlier mods are shown under the examples and passed to every new build.

![The New mod composer with example ideas and the lessons the fixer has learned so far](docs/images/new-mod.png)

## What happens next

1. **Spec agent** (Claude Opus) turns the sentence into behavior rules and an in-game **test plan** with measurable expectations, for example "the husk's upward velocity exceeds 0.8 blocks/tick".
2. **Builder** (Claude Code, Opus) implements the plugin in its own git repository created from `templates/paper-plugin`, and Maven builds it.
3. **Deploy**: Benana restarts its local Paper 1.21.4 server with the new jar, which takes about 16 seconds.
4. **Playtester** (Claude Code, Sonnet) controls `BenanaBot`, a real player, through the `minecraft` MCP tools: equip, attack, use items, and track an entity's velocity tick by tick. It reports pass, fail, or blocked for each check, with the measurements as evidence.
5. **Fixer** (Claude Code, Opus) receives the verdict, server stack traces, the mod's Entire checkpoint history, and the Neatlogs trace of the failed playtest. It fixes the root cause, writes down a **lesson**, and the loop runs again (up to 3 attempts).

## Watch the AI player test it

The live view is a real Minecraft 1.21.4 client, spectating next to BenanaBot, so you see the playtest with the game's own rendering: particles, lightning, the mod's textures and boss bars. The bot gets the item, spawns a target, and uses the mod on it. The server log streams next to it, so plugin errors are visible as they happen.

## Play it yourself

**Play in Minecraft** opens a second real Minecraft window and drops you into the same world, next to the bot, holding the mod's items (and husk eggs for targets). Benana downloads the vanilla client files from Mojang the first time and joins Benana's local server with them. Set `BENANA_PLAYER_NAME` in `.env` to pick your name.

![Three frames from BenanaBot's first-person view as it fights husks in the test arena](docs/images/live-view.png)

## When a playtest fails, it fixes itself

A failed check is not the end of the run. Every attempt keeps the measured evidence, the agent sessions behind it, and the fixer's lesson.

The **Mods** page below shows ArrowTracer, a real run that needed three attempts. The request was "can't see the arrows being shot". The first build reported the arrow's landing spot 1.3 blocks from the shooter instead of 7 to 9. The fixer traced the impact point along the arrow's velocity and wrote that down as a lesson. The second playtest still failed. On the third attempt the fixer worked out that the plugin was right: the husk had walked up to the bot before the shot. It fixed the test target by giving it NoAI, and all four checks passed. Total cost: $1.32.

![The Mods page: ArrowTracer's spec and its attempt timeline, with failed attempts, evidence and the fixer's lesson](docs/images/mods.png)

## Every agent session is traced (Neatlogs)

Every builder, playtester, and fixer session is traced through `@neatlogs/claude-code` hooks installed into each mod repository. The **Neatlogs** page lists all sessions across all mods. Opening one shows its cost, tokens, the failure it was handed, each tool call, and its final output. The fixer reads the failed playtest's trace before it changes any code.

![The Neatlogs page with the ArrowTracer fixer session open: duration, tokens, cost, the attempt 2 failure it received, and its 7 steps](docs/images/neatlogs-trace.png)

## Every commit is tied to its session (Entire)

Each agent commit in a mod repository carries an `Entire-Checkpoint` trailer that links the code to the session that wrote it. The **Entire** page shows the commit history per mod: builder, playtest, and fixer commits in order, with the checkpoint that produced each one. The fixer gets this history as context.

![The Entire page: ArrowTracer's six commits, alternating fixer attempts and playtests, each linked to a checkpoint](docs/images/entire.png)

## Insights

The **Insights** page tracks build outcomes, pass rate, first-try passes, and spend broken down by agent role and model.

![The Insights page: mods built, pass rate, agent sessions, total spend, build activity and spend by agent role](docs/images/insights.png)

## Partner tools

- **Neatlogs** traces every agent session (see above).
- **Entire** checkpoints every attempt (see above). This repository has Entire enabled too.
- **cfo.ai** holds the business plan: [docs/hackathon/cfo-plan.md](docs/hackathon/cfo-plan.md).

## Run it

Requirements: Node 22+ on `PATH` (the game bot runs on system Node), JDK 21, Maven 3.9, and Claude Code logged in. Install the [Entire CLI](https://github.com/entireio/cli) and `npm i -g @neatlogs/claude-code` for partner evidence.

```sh
npm ci
cp .env.example .env     # add Neatlogs keys
npm run dev
```

Click **Start game**, describe a mod, and press Enter. On first start Benana downloads Paper (51 MB). Game data lives in `~/.benana/game`, mod repositories in `~/.benana/mods`.

- `BENANA_GAME_AUTOSTART=1` starts the game with the app. `BENANA_GAME_DEMO=1` turns on attract mode, where the bot keeps launching husks. `BENANA_VIEW=first` switches the live view to the bot's first-person camera.
- **Seeded bug** (the toggle under the prompt) starts from `fixtures/seeded`, a labeled LaunchSword with the knockback bug. The playtester and fixer still run for real, and the UI labels the run as seeded.
- If Electron crashes at startup with `reading 'handle'`, unset `ELECTRON_RUN_AS_NODE`.

```sh
npm run build
npm test
```

Architecture and interfaces: [docs/hackathon/CONTRACTS.md](docs/hackathon/CONTRACTS.md). Build plan: [docs/hackathon/PLAN.md](docs/hackathon/PLAN.md). The original repository-bug workspace is still available from **Repository workspace** in the sidebar; see [execute_yourself.md](execute_yourself.md).

## Marketplace, hosted on Entire

The **Marketplace** lists published mods with their version, checkpoint count, remixes and playtest result. A published version is pushed to an Entire repository together with only the checkpoints behind it, so each listing shows the agent history that produced the mod.

![The ExplosiveArrows listing: two checkpoints recorded by Entire, hosted on Entire at /et/benana-market/explosive-arrows, playtest passed, and a Remix v2 button](docs/images/marketplace.png)

**Remix** starts a new mod from any published checkpoint. Benana clones the listing from Entire, checks out that checkpoint's commit, and seeds the new mod with the parent's spec, test plan, attempts and lessons. The next agent starts where the last one finished, and the remix is published as its own listing.

![A remix of ExplosiveArrows v2 at checkpoint 01M4MQJW8T, cloned from Entire, with the parent's four test checks inherited](docs/images/remix.png)

The publishing, privacy and remix design, including what was tested against the Entire CLI, is in [docs/marketplace/SPEC.md](docs/marketplace/SPEC.md).

## Creator CFO, powered by cfo.ai

The **CFO** page keeps books for every mod from the agents' recorded usage: build cost, money spent on fix attempts, first-try pass rate, and how many sales at $1.99 pay a mod back. **Ask your CFO** answers pricing, budget and runway questions by calling the creator's cfo.ai model over its MCP server, and shows each cfo.ai call it made. **Quote a mod before you build it** estimates a new idea's cost from the most similar past builds and how often they needed fixes, so creators can check whether a mod is worth building first.

![The CFO page: $13.01 recorded spend, 21% on rework, 53% passed first try, a cfo.ai answer pricing ThunderHammer at $1.99 (pays back in 2 sales), and a $2.29 quote for a dragon pet mod](docs/images/cfo.png)

## Insights

## How the launch video was made

The launch video is a [Remotion](https://www.remotion.dev) project in [`launch-video/`](launch-video). The motion graphics are React components. The app and game footage are real recordings, captured by scripts while the agents worked.

| Path | What it is |
|---|---|
| [`src/Launch.jsx`](launch-video/src/Launch.jsx) | The 70-second edit: the pain of modding by hand, the build, getting stuck and fixing itself, the marketplace, building in public, the CFO, and the outro |
| [`src/scenes/`](launch-video/src/scenes) | One component per beat, using real data: ArrowTracer's failed check (1.3 blocks measured vs 6–14 expected), ExplosiveArrows' Entire checkpoint IDs, and the CFO page's numbers |
| [`src/Logo.jsx`](launch-video/src/Logo.jsx) | The Benana logo: a pixel banana that assembles itself block by block, plus the wordmark |
| [`src/timeline.json`](launch-video/src/timeline.json) | The cut points in seconds, shared by the video and the music so cuts land on the beat |
| [`music.cjs`](launch-video/music.cjs) | Writes the soundtrack (`public/music.wav`) from code: 120 BPM, a ticking intro, a drop on the logo, a breakdown while the agent is stuck |
| [`obs.mjs`](launch-video/obs.mjs) | Drives OBS over obs-websocket: sets up 1080p scenes for the app window and the Minecraft client, then starts and stops named recordings |
| [`scrollto.mjs`](launch-video/scrollto.mjs), [`win.mjs`](launch-video/win.mjs) | Drive the dev app over the DevTools protocol (`BENANA_CDP_PORT`) during a recording |
| [`cut.sh`](launch-video/cut.sh) | Cuts and speeds up the raw recordings in `footage/` into the clips in `public/footage/` |
| [`public/logos/`](launch-video/public/logos) | Partner logos for Neatlogs, Entire and cfo.ai |

```sh
cd launch-video
npm ci
node music.cjs            # regenerate the soundtrack
npx remotion studio       # preview and edit
npx remotion render Launch out/benana-launch.mp4
```

Recording needs OBS with its websocket server turned on (port 4455) and the dev app started with `BENANA_CDP_PORT=9333`.

# Benana Mod Studio

Describe a Minecraft mod in one sentence. Benana writes it as a Paper plugin, starts a Minecraft server inside the app, and sends an AI player in to test it. When the playtest fails, a fixer agent reads the in-game evidence, patches the plugin, and the AI player tests it again. Finished mods go on a marketplace hosted on Entire, where anyone can remix them from any checkpoint, and a CFO backed by cfo.ai tells creators what a mod costs and what to charge for it.

[![Watch the 70-second launch video](docs/images/launch-video.png)](launch-video/out/benana-launch.mp4)

**[Watch the launch video](launch-video/out/benana-launch.mp4)** (70 s, 1080p). Every shot of the app and the game is a real recording; see [How the launch video was made](#how-the-launch-video-was-made).

![Benana Mod Studio: the agent's report on the left, the live game, server log, Neatlogs traces and Entire checkpoints on the right](docs/images/build.png)

## Start with one sentence

> "A golden sword that launches any mob it hits into the sky with particles, with a 3 second cooldown."

Type an idea, or pick one of the examples, and press Enter. You never open an IDE, a server console, or the game client. Lessons the fixer has learned from earlier mods are shown under the examples and passed to every new build.

![The New mod composer with example ideas and the lessons the fixer has learned so far](docs/images/new-mod.png)

## What happens next

1. **Spec agent** (Claude Opus) turns the sentence into behavior rules and an in-game **test plan** with measurable expectations, for example "the husk's upward velocity exceeds 0.8 blocks/tick".
2. **Builder** (Claude Code, Opus) implements the plugin in its own git repository created from `templates/paper-plugin`, and Maven builds it.
3. **Deploy**: Benana restarts its local Paper 1.21.4 server with the new jar, which takes about 16 seconds.
4. **Playtester** (Claude Code, Sonnet) controls `BenanaBot`, a real player, through the `minecraft` MCP tools: equip, attack, use items, and track an entity's velocity tick by tick. It reports pass, fail, or blocked for each check, with the measurements as evidence.
5. **Fixer** (Claude Code, Opus) receives the verdict, server stack traces, the mod's Entire checkpoint history, and the Neatlogs trace of the failed playtest. It fixes the root cause, writes down a **lesson**, and the loop runs again (up to 3 attempts).

## Watch the AI player test it

The live view is a real Minecraft 1.21.4 client, spectating next to BenanaBot, so you see the playtest with the game's own rendering: particles, lightning, the mod's textures and boss bars. The bot gets the item, spawns a target, and uses the mod on it. The server log streams next to it, so plugin errors are visible as they happen.

## Play it yourself

**Play in Minecraft** opens a second real Minecraft window and drops you into the same world, next to the bot, holding the mod's items (and husk eggs for targets). Benana downloads the vanilla client files from Mojang the first time and joins Benana's local server with them. Set `BENANA_PLAYER_NAME` in `.env` to pick your name.

![Three frames from BenanaBot's first-person view as it fights husks in the test arena](docs/images/live-view.png)

## When a playtest fails, it fixes itself

A failed check is not the end of the run. Every attempt keeps the measured evidence, the agent sessions behind it, and the fixer's lesson.

The **Mods** page below shows ArrowTracer, a real run that needed three attempts. The request was "can't see the arrows being shot". The first build reported the arrow's landing spot 1.3 blocks from the shooter instead of 7 to 9. The fixer traced the impact point along the arrow's velocity and wrote that down as a lesson. The second playtest still failed. On the third attempt the fixer worked out that the plugin was right: the husk had walked up to the bot before the shot. It fixed the test target by giving it NoAI, and all four checks passed. Total cost: $1.32.

![The Mods page: ArrowTracer's spec and its attempt timeline, with failed attempts, evidence and the fixer's lesson](docs/images/mods.png)

## Every agent session is traced (Neatlogs)

Every builder, playtester, and fixer session is traced through `@neatlogs/claude-code` hooks installed into each mod repository. The **Neatlogs** page lists all sessions across all mods. Opening one shows its cost, tokens, the failure it was handed, each tool call, and its final output. The fixer reads the failed playtest's trace before it changes any code.

![The Neatlogs page with the ArrowTracer fixer session open: duration, tokens, cost, the attempt 2 failure it received, and its 7 steps](docs/images/neatlogs-trace.png)

## Every commit is tied to its session (Entire)

Each agent commit in a mod repository carries an `Entire-Checkpoint` trailer that links the code to the session that wrote it. The **Entire** page shows the commit history per mod: builder, playtest, and fixer commits in order, with the checkpoint that produced each one. The fixer gets this history as context.

![The Entire page: ArrowTracer's six commits, alternating fixer attempts and playtests, each linked to a checkpoint](docs/images/entire.png)

## Marketplace, hosted on Entire

The **Marketplace** lists published mods with their version, checkpoint count, remixes and playtest result. A published version is pushed to an Entire repository together with only the checkpoints behind it, so each listing shows the agent history that produced the mod.

![The ExplosiveArrows listing: two checkpoints recorded by Entire, hosted on Entire at /et/benana-market/explosive-arrows, playtest passed, and a Remix v2 button](docs/images/marketplace.png)

**Remix** starts a new mod from any published checkpoint. Benana clones the listing from Entire, checks out that checkpoint's commit, and seeds the new mod with the parent's spec, test plan, attempts and lessons. The next agent starts where the last one finished, and the remix is published as its own listing.

![A remix of ExplosiveArrows v2 at checkpoint 01M4MQJW8T, cloned from Entire, with the parent's four test checks inherited](docs/images/remix.png)

The publishing, privacy and remix design, including what was tested against the Entire CLI, is in [docs/marketplace/SPEC.md](docs/marketplace/SPEC.md).

## Creator CFO, powered by cfo.ai

The **CFO** page keeps books for every mod from the agents' recorded usage: build cost, money spent on fix attempts, first-try pass rate, and how many sales at $1.99 pay a mod back. **Ask your CFO** answers pricing, budget and runway questions by calling the creator's cfo.ai model over its MCP server, and shows each cfo.ai call it made. **Quote a mod before you build it** estimates a new idea's cost from the most similar past builds and how often they needed fixes, so creators can check whether a mod is worth building first.

![The CFO page: $13.01 recorded spend, 21% on rework, 53% passed first try, a cfo.ai answer pricing ThunderHammer at $1.99 (pays back in 2 sales), and a $2.29 quote for a dragon pet mod](docs/images/cfo.png)

## Insights

The **Insights** page tracks build outcomes, pass rate, first-try passes, and spend broken down by agent role and model.

![The Insights page: mods built, pass rate, agent sessions, total spend, build activity and spend by agent role](docs/images/insights.png)

## Partner tools

- **Neatlogs** traces every agent session (see above).
- **Entire** checkpoints every attempt (see above). This repository has Entire enabled too.
- **cfo.ai** holds the business plan: [docs/hackathon/cfo-plan.md](docs/hackathon/cfo-plan.md).

## Run it

Requirements: Node 22+ on `PATH` (the game bot runs on system Node), JDK 21, Maven 3.9, and Claude Code logged in. Install the [Entire CLI](https://github.com/entireio/cli) and `npm i -g @neatlogs/claude-code` for partner evidence.

```sh
npm ci
cp .env.example .env     # add Neatlogs keys
npm run dev
```

Click **Start game**, describe a mod, and press Enter. On first start Benana downloads Paper (51 MB). Game data lives in `~/.benana/game`, mod repositories in `~/.benana/mods`.

- `BENANA_GAME_AUTOSTART=1` starts the game with the app. `BENANA_GAME_DEMO=1` turns on attract mode, where the bot keeps launching husks. `BENANA_VIEW=first` switches the live view to the bot's first-person camera.
- **Seeded bug** (the toggle under the prompt) starts from `fixtures/seeded`, a labeled LaunchSword with the knockback bug. The playtester and fixer still run for real, and the UI labels the run as seeded.
- If Electron crashes at startup with `reading 'handle'`, unset `ELECTRON_RUN_AS_NODE`.

```sh
npm run build
npm test
```

Architecture and interfaces: [docs/hackathon/CONTRACTS.md](docs/hackathon/CONTRACTS.md). Build plan: [docs/hackathon/PLAN.md](docs/hackathon/PLAN.md). The original repository-bug workspace is still available from **Repository workspace** in the sidebar; see [execute_yourself.md](execute_yourself.md).
